analysis.one_liner: Permanently exempts estates up to $5 million and cuts tax rates on larger estates.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 269-156 on June 22, 2006, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made permanent the estate tax cuts from the 2001 Bush tax law, which were scheduled to expire. It exempts the first $5 million of an estate ($10 million for a married couple, using the unused exclusion of a deceased spouse) starting in 2010, taxes the rest at 15% up to $25 million and 30% above that, and makes those rules permanent rather than letting the estate tax fully return in 2011. It also adds a special tax deduction for timber gains and repeals the deduction estates could take for death taxes paid to states.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to very large estates. Under the 2001 law, estates under $2 million (rising to $3.5 million in 2009) were already exempt and the tax was set to disappear entirely in 2010 before returning in 2011. This bill made the reduced tax permanent, so the families of decedents dying after 2009 with estates above $5 million would owe far less — and could plan with certainty. Timber growers would gain a deduction worth 60% of certain timber gains through 2008.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the estate tax exclusion to $5 million per person beginning in 2010, indexed to inflation, meaning a married couple could shield $10 million using the deceased spouse's unused exclusion [S2][S3][S4].
Cuts the rate on taxable estates to 15% on the first $25 million and 30% above that — far below the top rate in effect at the time [S2][S3].
Removes the 2010 sunset of the 2001 tax law's estate provisions, making the reduced estate tax permanent instead of letting the tax return at higher rates in 2011 [S2][S3].

Lets heirs use the date-of-death fair market value of inherited property instead of the carryover basis rules otherwise scheduled to take effect, avoiding capital gains taxes on appreciation during the deceased's lifetime [S2][S3].
Allows an election to deduct 60% of qualified timber gain for tax years ending after enactment through 2008, available even to taxpayers who do not itemize [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Revenue from the estate tax falls on estates above the exemption — the largest private fortunes — so a permanent cut means that revenue must be made up by other taxpayers, added borrowing, or spending cuts. State governments also lose, because the bill repeals the deduction estates could take for death taxes paid to states after 2009.

drawbacks.text: The permanent revenue loss is borne by everyone else through higher deficits or pressure for other taxes, since the estate tax falls almost entirely on the largest estates [S2][S3].
The bill repeals the deduction for state death taxes paid after 2009, shifting costs onto state budgets [S2][S3].
The timber gain deduction is a targeted break for one industry, terminating after 2008 [S3][S4].

A good-faith concern behind estate tax relief — family farms and small businesses facing the tax — was largely already addressed by the existing rising exemption; this bill went well beyond relief for those cases, cutting rates on estates into the tens of millions [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit goes almost entirely to heirs of the largest estates, while the cost — lost federal revenue and reduced state revenue — spreads across everyone else. The $5 million/$10 million exemption is generous relative to the family-farm and small-business concerns that motivated estate tax relief, and the 15% rate on estates up to $25 million (indexed to just twice the capital gains rate above $25 million) is a deep cut aimed at the very top. The bill is honestly drafted and permanent, which supporters valued for planning certainty, but its costs and benefits are sharply skewed toward the wealthiest families.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 269-156 in June 2006, but it was placed on the Senate calendar and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced June 19, 2006, by Ways and Means Chairman Bill Thomas and referred to his committee [S1][S6].
The Rules Committee set up a floor debate, and on June 22 the House agreed to consider the bill, 238-188 — with 228 of 230 Republicans in favor and 187 of 201 Democrats opposed [S6][S7].

Democrats offered two motions to send the bill back to committee: Charles Rangel's was ruled out of order as non-germane, and Earl Pomeroy's substitute — which would have replaced the bill with different estate tax relief — failed 182-236, with 182 of 201 Democrats in favor and no Republicans [S6][S9].
The House passed the bill 269-156: 226 of 231 Republicans voted yes, 43 of 201 Democrats voted yes, and the lone Independent voted no [S6][S10].

The Senate received the bill on June 23 and placed it on the Senate calendar under General Orders on June 26; it never received a Senate vote, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the estate tax continued as scheduled and the federal Treasury kept revenue that only the largest estates would have paid. General taxpayers and state governments are better off than under the bill; heirs of very large estates, who would have paid less, are worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers, since the estate tax survived

for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee

for.name: 43 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage, supplying the margin that put the bill over the top

against.name: Earl Pomeroy
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions substituting different estate tax relief; the motion failed 182-236

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Ranking member, House Ways and Means Committee

against.role: Senators who had blocked estate tax repeal attempts earlier in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: The Senate never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; earlier in June 2006 Senate Republicans had failed to cut off debate on estate tax repeal, and the bill sat on the calendar until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous (226-2 on passage, 228-0 to consider the bill) while most Democrats opposed it (153-43 on passage), though the 43 Democratic yes votes were needed to reach the 269-vote total.

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest estates and wealthy families
industries.note: Estates above $5 million per person ($10 million per couple) would owe a permanently lower tax, with the 15% rate applying to estates up to $25 million. The revenue forgone must be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing.
The bill adds a deduction for 60% of qualified timber gain through 2008, a targeted tax break for one industry beyond the estate tax changes.

The bill repeals the deduction estates could claim for death taxes paid to states after 2009, and states had also relied on the federal estate tax framework for their own inheritance taxes. The lost revenue would come out of state budgets.
A permanent, low-rate estate tax with a $5 million exemption would reduce the need for the complex planning that a changing and uncertain estate tax generates.
